record.paper_title: Ductile-to-brittle transition and yielding in soft amorphous materials: perspectives and open questions
record.original_question: Which theoretical framework can correctly describe the ductile-to-brittle transition in soft amorphous materials: a critical-like statistical-mechanics framework for disordered systems, a dynamical or continuum framework such as fluidity models, or a synthesis of these approaches, and what measurable material properties and predictions can distinguish among them?

evidence.quote: This leads to the key physical question of determining the correct theoretical framework to describe the DBT: should the DBT be described based on critical-like phenomena in the framework of statistical mechanics of disordered systems, or based on dynamical approaches as proposed in continuous models? Then, one should focus on the possible predictions, if any , which can be obtained using the different tools, and on the material properties that one should consider relevant in order to test the various approaches.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a soft amorphous material (for example, a colloidal glass, emulsion, foam, gel, or other disordered solid) subjected to mechanical loading such as quasi-static or finite-rate shear deformation. Such materials are observed to yield either in a ductile manner (a smooth crossover between solid-like and flowing states) or in a brittle manner (an abrupt, often catastrophic stress drop accompanied by shear-band localization), with a ductile-to-brittle transition (DBT) controlled by parameters such as the degree of annealing, density of the disordered preparation, loading rate, and system size.

Two main classes of theoretical descriptions have been proposed:

(a) A statistical-mechanics framework treating yielding as a nonequilibrium phase transition in disordered systems, in which a critical-like point separates a regime of discontinuous (brittle) yielding from a regime of continuous (ductile) yielding, with associated diverging correlation lengths, finite-size scaling, and avalanche statistics.

(b) A dynamical/continuum framework, such as fluidity models, shear-transformation-zone theories, or elasto-plastic models with a structural order parameter (fluidity) whose coupled evolution with stress and strain rate produces shear localization, hysteresis, and a transition between homogeneous and banded flow.

The problem is:

1. Determine which (if either) of frameworks (a) and (b), or a synthesis of the two, correctly describes the ductile-to-brittle transition in soft amorphous materials, in the sense of reproducing the experimentally observed phenomenology across the relevant range of materials and protocols.

2. Identify quantitative predictions—such as critical exponents, scaling of avalanche sizes and shear-band widths with system size and strain rate, behavior of fluidity and its relaxation time near yielding, dependence of yield stress and yield strain on annealing depth, and statistics of stress drops—that differ between frameworks (a) and (b) and can in principle be measured.

3. Specify the material properties (e.g. preparation protocol, interaction potential, packing fraction, polydispersity, aging time, elastic moduli, characteristic relaxation times) that must be controlled or characterized in experiments and simulations in order to discriminate among the candidate frameworks.
artifact.status_search_result: The question is explicitly framed as an open problem in a 2024 Soft Matter review on the ductile-to-brittle transition in soft amorphous materials. While there is substantial progress—e.g. identification of a random critical point separating brittle and ductile yielding in well-annealed glasses (Ozawa et al., PNAS 2018) and recent simulation work on activity-induced annealing (Nature Physics 2024)—no single theoretical framework has been established as definitive, and competing statistical-mechanical and continuum/fluidity descriptions remain under active investigation.

status_evidence.title: Random critical point separates brittle and ductile yielding transitions in amorphous materials
status_evidence.snippet: well-annealed systems yield discontinuously...the transition terminates in a second-order critical point...poorly annealed systems yielding becomes a smooth crossover
status_evidence.claim: Provides partial evidence supporting a critical-point statistical-mechanics description, but does not settle the synthesis with fluidity models.

status_evidence.title: Activity-induced annealing leads to a ductile-to-brittle transition in amorphous solids
status_evidence.snippet: activity-induced annealing leads to a ductile-to-brittle transition
status_evidence.claim: Recent (2024) work continues to probe mechanisms of the DBT, indicating ongoing theoretical investigation.
